title: Agent Guardrails, NeMo & Code Sandboxing
summary: Study NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails as a concrete implementation of policy checkpoints, repair an offline guarded internal-API bridge, and compare containers, gVisor, and Firecracker microVMs as containment boundaries. The general authorization and containment principles transfer across model providers; NeMo configuration and rail behavior are implementation-specific.
objectives: Map input, retrieval, dialog, execution, and output rails to the stage of an LLM interaction each inspects, and name the failure modes guardrails themselves introduce.

Apply NeMo Guardrails' integration guidelines -- model output treated as untrusted, calls made in the user's authorization context, credentials isolated from the model, allow-lists that fail closed -- to a tool-calling design.
Repair a tool bridge that incorrectly treats a guardrail allow decision as authorization, then verify independent session, tenant, action, approval, budget, output, and audit controls.
Compare container, gVisor, and Firecracker isolation by what each places between untrusted code and the host kernel, and by what each still relies on the host to enforce.
Compose execution-time guardrails with a sandbox so that each layer catches what the other cannot, and test the composition with planted failures.

sections.title: Guardrails are checkpoints in a request flow
paragraphs: NVIDIA's NeMo Guardrails library is an open-source Python package for blocking, altering, or validating unsafe, off-topic, malicious, or policy-violating user inputs and model responses. It uses rails, YAML configuration, Colang flows, custom Python actions, and runtime interfaces including a Python SDK and guardrails server.

Input rails inspect a user message before the application LLM is called. Retrieval rails filter or transform retrieved chunks. Dialog rails use Colang flows to steer the conversation. Execution rails validate actions and tools, including inputs and outputs. Output rails inspect a generated response before it reaches the user. Input and output rails are common, so retrieval and execution are important places to check for an unguarded path.

A rail is a policy checkpoint, not authorization and not containment. It judges content that passes through it and constrains nothing that bypasses it. A classifier can also miss adversarial wording. This lesson's fixture intentionally allows the phrase "neighboring account" even though the resulting customer lookup crosses a tenant boundary. The independent execution-time authorization check must still deny that lookup.

NeMo's guidelines identify over-aggressive blocking, overgeneralized canonical forms, and model nondeterminism as failure modes. Flow logic can avoid unnecessary checks, while evaluation and regression tests are needed to expose false positives and false negatives. These cautions apply whether the application calls an OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, open-weight, or other model. The provider-neutral principle is to distrust model output; the specific YAML, Colang, and rail interfaces described here are NVIDIA NeMo features.

code.label: Sending messages through a guardrailed interface (from the NeMo Guardrails overview)
code.code:
from nemoguardrails import LLMRails, RailsConfig

config = RailsConfig.from_path("./config")
rails = LLMRails(config)

response = rails.generate(
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
)

sections.title: The golden rule for tool integrations
paragraphs: NeMo's security guidelines say to consider the LLM to be like a web browser under the complete control of the user and to treat everything it generates as untrusted. A service must be invoked in the LLM user's authorization context. Ask whether you would deliberately expose the same resource and interface directly to the internet. If not, redesign the integration.

Keep authenticated session state outside model input. The model may propose a tool name and arguments, but it must not choose its effective subject, tenant, roles, approval state, credentials, or budget. At execution time, the bridge loads a server-side session and independently checks the resource and action. A guardrail allow decision is only one input to that process.

Use a tool and schema allow-list, reject unknown properties, validate results, keep secrets outside the prompt, and fail closed. Errors returned to the model should not reveal an internal API's existence or the detailed authorization reason. Audit records may retain a redacted reason for authorized operators, but must not contain tokens, customer secrets, or raw service results.

Useful audit evidence connects the triggering text, parsed call, authentication method and time, authorization decision, downstream call and summarized result, and reinsertion decision. Safe limits must be checked before work begins. Arithmetic must use bounded safe integers, approval times must be validated, and a revoked or expired approval must never be accepted.

Execution rails are appropriate checkpoints for tool calls, but they cannot constrain what arbitrary code does after it starts. Conversely, an OS sandbox cannot repair an over-privileged internal API call that never enters the sandbox.
sections.callout: A guardrail may say whether a proposal looks acceptable. Only the trusted execution boundary can decide whether this authenticated user may perform this action on this resource.

sections.title: Worked example: follow one cross-tenant proposal
paragraphs: The supplied lab has synthetic tenants blue and amber. Session sess-blue-reader is loaded by trusted application code and belongs to subject user-blue in tenant blue. The model proposal asks for customer.read on customer amber-1 and says "summarize the neighboring account." No session identity is accepted in the proposal.

The fixture guardrail misses that wording and returns allowed. The starter bridge contains the sole repair defect: it runs authorization only when the guardrail denies. Because this proposal was allowed, the starter reaches the synthetic internal API and exposes an amber-tenant record to a blue-tenant session.

The correct sequence is shape validation, guardrail decision, budget reservation, independent execution-time authorization, internal operation, result validation and redaction, then audit completion. Authorization must run for every proposal. With that sequence, customer amber-1 is resolved to tenant amber, compared with the server-side session tenant blue, and denied before any customer result is returned.

The model receives only {"ok":false,"error":"request_denied"}. A redacted operator audit event records decision "deny" and reasonCode "TENANT_MISMATCH" without a token or customer record. This is causal defense: the denial is caused by comparing trusted session context with trusted resource ownership, not by hoping the guardrail recognizes every cross-tenant phrase.

code.label: The focused repair

sections.title: Choosing an isolation boundary for model-written code
paragraphs: A Docker container uses host-kernel namespaces for process and network isolation and cgroups for resource accounting and limits. Cgroups are not data isolation. Containers share the host kernel, and Docker warns that capabilities and mounts affect the boundary. Access to the Docker daemon is privileged control-plane access and must not be given to model-written code.

gVisor places its Go application kernel, the Sentry, between the workload and a restricted host interface. The Sentry services application system calls rather than passing them directly through to the host. File access beyond the sandbox is handled through the Gofer. The documented trade-offs include reduced compatibility and system-call overhead. gVisor uses host cgroups for resources and still depends on the host and platform for matters such as side-channel defenses.

Firecracker uses KVM microVMs with a minimal virtual device model. Its jailer can establish cgroups and a chroot, drop privileges, and run Firecracker as an unprivileged process. Firecracker applies seccomp filters and supports per-device rate limits. Its design does not filter guest network traffic, so operators must treat egress as untrusted and enforce network policy on the host.

The boundaries therefore differ: a container places namespaces and cgroups around a process that still uses the host kernel; gVisor interposes a userspace application kernel and Gofer before a restricted host interface; Firecracker places a guest kernel and virtual hardware boundary on KVM inside a jailer. All still depend on a trusted host and control plane. Egress, resource configuration, image and kernel provenance, logging, and access to runtime administration remain operator responsibilities.

sections.title: A sandbox is not a substitute for a secure architecture
paragraphs: A sandbox cannot help when an allowed tool directly invokes an over-privileged internal API. That is the lab's non-sandbox bypass: customer.export is an ordinary fixture operation, not generated code. It must still be stopped when the session lacks the action or when its approval is revoked.

Compose layers. Before execution, validate the proposal and authorize its resource and action. During actual code execution, use an OS isolation boundary with no credentials, filtered egress, resource limits, and inaccessible runtime control plane. After execution, validate and redact results before reinsertion. Log enough redacted evidence to reconstruct the path.

The JavaScript lab simulates a guardrail, session store, internal API, and execution policy. It does not execute arbitrary supplied code and is not an OS sandbox. Passing its tests establishes only the fixture policy behavior. It provides no Docker, gVisor, Firecracker, benchmark, production, or containment evidence.

Optional host probes are separately documented in HOST-ISOLATION.md. Their status remains UNVERIFIED until run on an approved Linux host satisfying every prerequisite. A skipped or unsupported probe is SKIP, never PASS.

sections.title: Repair lab: authorization is independent of guardrail classification
paragraphs: Open the lab at https://github.com/project42dev/project42-content/tree/main/training/ai-security-and-governance/guardrails-and-sandboxing/lab/ and work from the repository root. The offline core requires Node.js 22 and no package installation.

Run node training/ai-security-and-governance/guardrails-and-sandboxing/lab/reset.mjs, then run node training/ai-security-and-governance/guardrails-and-sandboxing/lab/tests/run-tests.mjs starter. The initial suite gathers every result and exits 1. Repair only src/bridge.mjs. Do not weaken contracts, tests, fixture ownership, approval checks, audit redaction, or budgets.

The repaired bridge must authorize every guardrail-allowed proposal using the server-side session and resource records. Run the same command until it prints 8 passed, 0 failed and exits 0. Compare behavior, not source text, with node training/ai-security-and-governance/guardrails-and-sandboxing/lab/tests/run-tests.mjs reference.

For the independent changed-input variation, run node training/ai-security-and-governance/guardrails-and-sandboxing/lab/tests/variation.mjs starter. It uses a different session, tenant, customer, wording, and revoked approval. Passing the original cases without the same authorization invariant will not pass this variation.
sections.callout: Do not copy the reference file into the starter. The rubric rewards the invariant: every proposal is independently authorized at the bridge, even when a guardrail allows it.

sections.title: Causal feedback and rubric
paragraphs: If action substitution fails, the bridge executed customer.export even though the authenticated session lacked that action. Cause: authorization was skipped or trusted the proposal. If cross-tenant denial logging fails, the bridge failed to compare trusted resource ownership with the trusted session or failed to record the denial. If revoked approval fails, the bridge treated a past approval as current or skipped approval policy.

If forged subject or tenant fails, a model-controlled identity property reached policy evaluation. Cause: unknown properties were accepted or identity was derived from model arguments. If result leakage fails, raw internal fields escaped output validation. If budget exhaustion fails, work continued after bounded server-side quota was consumed.

Rubric, 10 points: 4 points for unconditional independent authorization before the internal operation; 2 points for preserving session-bound identity, resource ownership, action, and approval checks; 1 point for preserving strict contracts and output redaction; 1 point for preserving budget enforcement and redacted denial audit events; 1 point for passing the independent changed-input variation; 1 point for accurately explaining why the fixture is not sandbox evidence. Any solution that authorizes from model-supplied identity, disables a test, turns SKIP into PASS, or evaluates arbitrary supplied code receives no credit for the affected criterion.

activity.title: Repair and explain a guarded execution path
instructions: From the repository root, reset the lab and run the starter suite. Record the exact three failing cases and connect each failure to the incorrect conditional in src/bridge.mjs.
Repair only the focused authorization defect. Require independent session, resource, action, and approval authorization for every proposal, including proposals the guardrail allows.
Run the immutable gather-all suite and the independent changed-input variation. Compare with the separate reference implementation.
Explain how the forged subject and tenant cases prove that model arguments cannot establish identity, and how the cross-tenant case proves that a guardrail allow is not authorization.
Explain why customer.export is a non-sandbox path and why the JavaScript fixture provides no OS containment evidence.

Choose container, gVisor, or Firecracker for a hypothetical generated-code worker. Name what sits between the workload and host kernel, then list host-owned egress, resource, side-channel, and control-plane dependencies.
Optionally follow HOST-ISOLATION.md on an approved host. Report PASS, FAIL, SKIP, or UNVERIFIED exactly as observed and do not infer production containment from a probe.
evidence: The repaired src/bridge.mjs and unmodified immutable tests.
Exact stdout and exit status for starter, repaired starter, reference, and independent variation commands.
A causal explanation for forged identity, action substitution, result leakage, denial logging, budget exhaustion, and revoked approval.
An isolation-boundary decision record naming host-enforced dependencies and owners.
If optional probes were run, their command transcript and status; otherwise an explicit UNVERIFIED statement.
activity.reflectionPrompt: If the guardrail missed every cross-tenant phrase, which trusted comparison would still stop access, and where must that comparison execute?

questions.prompt: In NeMo Guardrails, which rail type validates tool and action calls, including their inputs and outputs?
choices: Input rails
Dialog rails
Execution rails
Output rails
questions.explanation: Execution rails validate and control custom actions and tools, including their inputs and outputs; input and output rails inspect the user message and the model response.

questions.prompt: NeMo's golden rule for LLM integrations says any service the model invokes must be invoked in which context?
choices: The context of the LLM user
A shared service account with administrator rights, for reliability
The model provider's identity
An anonymous context, so no identity can leak
questions.explanation: The guidelines treat the model as a browser under the user's complete control and require every invoked service to run in the user's authorization context.

questions.prompt: An internal API call fails because the user lacks authorization. According to NeMo's guidelines, what should the response to the model reveal?
choices: The external API name and the exact authorization error, for debuggability
The missing role, so the user can request it
Nothing that identifies which API was called or why it failed
The full stack trace
questions.explanation: Fail gracefully and secretly: errors are trapped and rewritten so a user cannot detect that an internal API exists or learn why a call failed.

questions.prompt: What happens when an application running in a gVisor sandbox makes a system call?
choices: It is passed through to the host kernel after a seccomp check
The Sentry services it with its own implementation and does not pass it through to the host
It is translated into a hardware virtualization trap handled by a full guest OS
It is logged and allowed
questions.explanation: The Sentry is an application kernel that implements system calls itself; file operations beyond the sandbox go to the Gofer, and the Sentry's own host access is restricted.

questions.prompt: Firecracker's design document says what about network traffic leaving a guest microVM?
choices: Firecracker filters it against an allow-list by default
The jailer inspects every packet
Firecracker performs no traffic filtering; all guest egress is untrusted and should be filtered at the host
Egress is impossible because microVMs have no network device
questions.explanation: Firecracker applies I/O rate limiting but no network filtering, so egress control is a host responsibility the operator must own.

questions.prompt: After combining several NeMo rails, a team sees safe requests blocked. What remedy do NeMo's guidelines suggest?
choices: Remove all output rails
Use flow logic to avoid unnecessary calls, for example running fact-checking only on factual questions
Raise the model temperature
Move every check into the system prompt
questions.explanation: Over-aggressive moderation is more likely when guardrails are combined; the documented remedy is flow logic that reduces unnecessary rail calls, backed by evaluation and regression testing.
